utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before the Defence calls its next expert witness, the Chamber would like to deal with the documents that have been tendered during the -- through the expert witness Professor Vilicic. Madam Registrar, could you assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit C5, Chamber exhibit, diagram drawn by Dr. Vilicic; MFI 30, diagram drawn by Judge Orie; D1848, photo documentation; Exhibit P3801, Sandia National Laboratories report; Exhibit P3802, fragmentation of a mortar shell; Exhibit P3800, recording of the burst of an HE projectile process; Exhibit P3799, marked photocopy of portion of Exhibit C2; P3806, photo of fuses; P3803, P3804, and P3805, maps of confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could I please see those items that were only recently provided with a number, that is, especially MFI 30. Yes, that's MFI 30. And C5, yes. Thank you. Since I hear no objections, these documents are either admitted into evidence or, as far as marked for identification, are identified. We'll deal with the videos later this week as soon as the copies have been prepared, the -- I'm talking about the videos provided by -- parts, excerpts of the videos provided by Mr. Gray. Is there any other procedural issue that would need immediate attention? I am aware that last Friday, when you, Mr. Ierace, asked to raise one or two issues, one of them being urgent, that I did not give you the opportunity finally. And so if there's any issue that should be raised, you have an opportunity now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before senior counsel proceeds, may I be allowed to withdraw, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity, Mr. President. As the end of the Defence case draws near, there are two issues which may be thought to be unresolved, not only now but regardless of whatever verdict is handed down, perhaps ultimately by the Appeals Chamber, if ever this matter should surface there. The first concerns the application by the Defence for the issue of subpoena in respect of certain witnesses. While I'm aware that some steps have been taken to secure their attendance, if they do not attend or indeed if any of them do not attend, that application stands on the record apparently without a formal response. The second issue concerns the oral decision of the Trial Chamber of the 22nd of January, 2003, concerning the stage of the trial at which the accused could give evidence. I note that the time indicated for the accused to be called has passed and that the Defence case is likely to conclude in the next week or so, unless some further UN witnesses of fact are called. I also note that a witness of fact has already been called during the expert testimony segment of the Defence case, namely Richard Gray. The Defence may take the view that because of the terms of the oral order and the decision of the Trial Chamber to not issue a certificate for an appeal, that no aspect of the matter can be further raised. I submit that the Defence should indicate in clear terms to the Trial Chamber before the close of the Defence case what actual prejudice, if any, has been caused to the accused by the Trial Chamber's decision as to when the accused could have been called. By "actual prejudice" I do not mean any infringement of the accused's right to silence as perceived by the Defence but, rather, any substantive impact in an evidential sense on what the accused might have said or what topics his evidence would have concerned had he been called for the first time during or at the end of the expert witness testimony and which he did not reasonably anticipate at the beginning of the expert testimony. If this is done by the Defence, then the Prosecution can consider its position and the Trial Chamber is able to reconsider its oral decision, if it thinks it appropriate. Mr. President, there is a third matter which arises from an observation made last night right at the end of Mr. Vilicic's testimony in relation to a document that Mr. Stamp sought to show to the witness. You, Mr. President, said: "These statements are not in evidence and I think it's quite clear that the Defence has presented material that was not in evidence and the Chamber, I think, earlier has made clear that an expert witness is not an instrument through which you introduce new evidence which has not been subject to cross-examination by the other party." Mr. President, in particular, in relation to the anticipated evidence of Mr. Radinovic, there have been, I think now, hundreds of documents provided by the Defence to the Prosecution; many of those are attached to the expert's report. There will not be enough time for the Prosecution to cross-examine Mr. Radinovic in relation to all of the documents that the Prosecution may wish to rely upon in its closing submission, in its closing brief. We had in mind that indeed many of these documents did not require any comment by the witness since they purported -- each document purported to speak for itself, subject to any authenticity issue. Therefore, we intended that we would incorporate some of that material or may incorporate some of that material in our closing brief but not require the witness to comment on them. I would be grateful, therefore, if we could have an indication before cross-examination of Mr. Radinovic as to whether this is acceptable to the Trial Chamber. It would assist us in structuring the cross-examination of that witness. And to assist you, it relates to documents which have been attached to the filed report, and therefore pursuant to the decision of the Trial Chamber have, as I understand it, already been admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all of this is a bit abstruse. First of all, one should be a little more clear because one has to deal with everything Mr. Ierace said. As far as the first issue is concerned, the Defence would appreciate it if Mr. Ierace could tell us which legal provisions he is basing himself on so that the Defence can avoid doing the exercise that he wants the Defence to do. What is the text, what are the violations that have are been resumed that the Prosecution is talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to the second point. You said the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are so many points, Mr. President, that I have difficulty in categorising them. But I'd like to know what the violations are, given the order of the presentation of the witnesses, et cetera. If this is the first or the eighteenth point, I don't know. But as far as this is concerned, it's often that the Defence cannot deal with this, since we're involved in preparation. To ask us to do so is not quite right. As far as the other issues are concerned, the matter of documents tendered by Mr. Stamp, in a surprising manner I have no comment to make. It's obvious that the Defence finds this unacceptable. It's not necessary to emphasise this. And as far as the other issues are concerned, the issues relating to the testimony of Mr. Radinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the documents tendered by Mr. Stamp. Which documents did you have in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were these documents which were tendered overnight. They were mentioned. I'm referring to what Mr. Ierace said a minute ago, with regard to the examination or the cross-examination of Mr. Vilicic. The Prosecution must know more about this than I do because the Prosecution mentioned these documents a minute Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ago, if I understood what the Prosecution was getting at. And, Mr. President, finally as far as the problem of the documents is concerned, the documents that concern Mr. Radinovic's expert report, we would like to emphasise the following: These documents in the hands of the Prosecution, they have been in their hands for a long time, with the exception perhaps of a map that was made by General Radinovic -- by Mr. Radinovic himself. But the basic documents are in their hands and they have been in their hands for a long time. A minute ago the Defence -- a while ago we suggested giving them a chronological plan of these documents so that they could find their bearings. We were quite happy to deal with this. But if the Prosecution has more time for preparations than we do, then one should be logical. If that is the case, we would require a break, each side would need to take advantage of a break. That would be the best means of respecting the balance of forces. These annexes, about 130 documents, these are documents which the Prosecution has always been familiar with, because to a large extent they were provided to us by the Prosecution itself. This is what we wanted to say relatively briefly, Mr. President. Obviously if there are other issues, we could examine them later on. But we don't think it's the right time to do so now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the documents tendered by Mr. Stamp. What Mr. Ierace said is that there was a matter "which arises from an observation made last night at the end of Mr. Vilicic's testimony in relation to a document that Mr. Stamp sought to show to the witness, and that the Chamber commented that this document was not in evidence and that the -- an expert witness was not the instrument through which one could introduce new witness statements." Your position in respect of that is not entirely clear to me, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Let's say that I'm following the way, the path of the Trial Chamber. And I'd like to also say that the 130 documents which form the annex of the expert report which are mentioned in this document - we're talking about General Radinovic's expert report the Defence considers them to be part of the expert report itself, and therefore that they should be provided as exhibits, as evidence before your Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your position in that respect. I have not heard your position in respect to the first question raised by the Prosecution. That was question of the motion for subpoenaing certain witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Before we examine the possibility of a request for a subpoena, I would like to literally exhaust all the possibilities that we have at our disposal, all the possible manners of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the motion to subpoena certain witnesses. I think that was the question, not on the possibility of a request, but on the outstanding request.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, I think that it's necessary to wait, if I may say so, in that we would like to see, the Defence, and General Galic would like to see, what the situation is now with regard to the documents that were already tendered and the testimonies we have heard, and we'll be able to provide an answer I think very soon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber responds to this first issue at this very moment. The others, we'll respond to that at a later moment, in due course. As far as the motion to subpoena certain witnesses are concerned, the Chamber, as may have been experienced by the parties, the Chamber has primarily oriented itself in assisting the Defence in getting these witnesses into this courtroom without, technically speaking, going in much detail in the merits of the motion as such, because the Chamber feels it an obligation to assist the parties as good as it can to get the witnesses into the courtroom, the witnesses the Defence seeks to examine. That means that we were not successful in all respects. I think there are two witnesses that did not appear that have not been withdrawn by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I do apologise. Given what the Defence has just said, might I respectfully make a suggestion before you give your -- deliver your observations in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd just let me finish for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, and if there would be any -- So that means that there are two witnesses that -- of which we do not know yet whether you still intend to call them and -- or whether you -- whether the Defence would withdraw its request then, in respect of subpoenaing these witnesses. There are two possibilities: Either you insist on the Chamber giving a decision. We'll then give a decision. And I do understand that you need some time to consider your position. If you insist on a decision, it will not be an outstanding motion without a decision. So then a decision will be given. We'll then go into the merits of the -- of the motion and we'll deliver a decision. If you withdraw it, it goes without saying that no decision will be delivered. The Chamber would like to hear within one or two days what your position is in respect of these two witnesses, one of Canadian, one of Indian nationality. Mr. Ierace, is there any need to ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Mr. President. To say this: It seems to me that the comments of Mr. Piletta-Zanin really amount to a withdrawal of the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I see, that he first wanted to confer with the accused and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thank the Prosecution for making this hermeneutic effort and to try to interpret myself, but I don't think that I'd managed to do that myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are always making great efforts in assisting each other, which of course is highly appreciated by the Chamber. The other issues will be dealt with at a later stage. Then is the Defence ready to call its next expert witness? I take it that will be Mr. Terzic. Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Terzic, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Before you'll be examined by counsel for the Defence, I would like to say to you that we are aware that you waited for a long time yesterday and in vain, because finally we could not start with your examination. We feel sorry for you that you had to wait such a long time and then had to return without even entering this courtroom yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, on Friday too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that -- I then have to underline this once Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. again. We really regret that this happened. Ms. Pilipovic. Examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Dr. Terzic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, before I ask you some questions about the statement that you have provided at the Defence's request, could you briefly tell us about your background, regardless of the fact that we provided a detailed curriculum vitae which was attached to your statement. Where were you born and where do you work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1949, in Pandurica near Pljevlja in Montenegro. I finished secondary school in Gorazde and Pljevlja, and I graduated from university in Belgrade. I graduated in national and general history. I obtained my masters and Ph.D. in Belgrade at the university. I am involved in the history of the Serbs, and of the Yugoslav areas, the Balkan area. I carried out research in big centres throughout the world, in Greece, in Germany and Russia. I've researched many archives in the former Yugoslavia and outside of the former Yugoslavia. And among other things, I have also carried out research in the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to say that I provided my curriculum vitae, and it just contains extracts from my works, some of my works. I have written about 150 studies, articles. I'd like to add that what I did not include there is that I am the editor of a large book, "Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Middle Ages up until the modern era." And I would be happy to provide the Trial Chamber here with this book as a present. I am also the editor of many other books, among which there is "The atlas of the Ustasha genocide against the Serbs, from 1941 to 1945,", and I'm also -- I'd like to underline this, a participant in an international meeting of historians, 1955-1956 [as interpreted] in Germany. It was organised by the German conference of bishops. This was a meeting of historians of Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim -- and German historians. I was also a member of the commission for South Slav history, the Pro Oriente from Vienna. And I'm also at the moment the president --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's a mistake in the transcript. I think Dr. Terzic said 1995 to 1996 and not 1955 to 1956.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's 1995 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you briefly tell us, because the Defence has only ten minutes for your examination. Can you just tell us where you work now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I worked as a secondary school professor for two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you work now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's going a bit too fast for the interpreters. Could you please make a short break before starting to answer the question. The best way of keeping control of your own speed is to look at the screen. As soon as it stops, the text stops moving, then the interpreters have translated your words. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Dr. Terzic, can you just tell us where you are employed now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I work in the historical institute in Belgrade. I've worked in that institute for over 25 years. For a long time it was part of the Serbian academy of science and arts. For six months now it hasn't been part of that. I was the director of the historical institute of Serbian science for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Terzic. At the Defence's request you provided a statement in which you dealt with the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you concentrated in particular on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you stand by everything that you stated in that report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by everything that I said. But there are three things I would like to add, if I may: Number one, when this was being typed out, there was a mistake, a minor mistake in the footnotes, in the number of the pages. So I would like to ask that to be changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Terzic, if you can be very brief. Can you tell us on which pages these changes should be made.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: It's footnote number 56. It should say "page 87" there, footnote page 58 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To help my colleagues, it's page 24 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I think it's possible to follow the footnotes too. So footnote 58, it should say "page 132." Footnote 59, "page 133." Footnote 62, "page 65 up to page 76." Footnote 63, "page 72, 73." And footnote 64, should be on page 135 to 137. That's one change, one correction. And the second addition, the second change has to do with the table on the structure of the population of Sarajevo according to the 1981 census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's page 21 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: When it was being typed out, information of two municipalities were left out. So in addition to the eight municipalities that are here, information for the municipality of Hadzici and the municipality of Ilijas was left out, and I would now like to add this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document be put on the ELMO, please, because the interpreters do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- although I, for the interpreters, I think as a matter of fact that the expert witness is going to add parts that are not contained in the document. But perhaps could we please have the document on the ELMO. And could you please assist, Mr. Usher, that -- if we put it on, to the right of you, we can all see it on the screen, Dr. Terzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So in addition to information on eight Sarajevo municipalities, which are here, there was no information for the municipality of Hadzici and for the municipality of Ilijas. The information for the Hadzici municipality states the following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Ms. Pilipovic. Would it not be a better idea to have a copy of these corrections made during the break so that we do not ask the interpreters to translate all these figures, with all the risks of mistakes. And therefore, would you be willing to give a corrected copy of that page to the registry, Dr. Terzic, so that it can be copied and we don't have to read aloud all these numbers? Would you agree that to be a more practical way of dealing with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course if you would like to comment on the new figures, that's a different matter. But Mr. Usher, perhaps then -- Unless you need it at this very moment, Dr. Terzic, or if you want to add anything. Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to comment on the information, demographic structure of the population and then later to provide you with this document to be photocopied. And I have a third addition. It's not a change but an addition. Page 50, and I believe that in English it is also page 50, I said that in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the 1992-1995 war, not less than 400 prisons and camps were registered. Meanwhile, I have expanded my investigation and concluded the number of camps and prisons for Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina totalled 536. I have here -- I have a map with camps and I have the list of all the camps and prisons which I can also give to be photocopied with the leave of the President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Terzic, as you were pointing out these misprints in your written statement, and you told us otherwise that you stood by it completely, my question would be: In view of the substance of your statement, to tell us -- when it comes to the historical demography, what is your conclusion about the basic features of the ethnic and religious structure in Bosnia-Herzegovina with special reference to Sarajevo? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: This is an important issue that I covered in detail. As a historian, I believe that the historical context is very important if one is to understand modern day political events. The historical experience, the historical traumas, the historical -- the past frustrations largely determined the political behaviour of individuals, groups, and nations as such. With regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina, if we follow the processes for the past 150 years, the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, since mid-nineteenth century - and it is to that period that Turkish censuses date back to, until the end of the twentieth century - looked more like this: Orthodox Serbs totalled about 47, 48 per cent in mid-century. Muslims accounted for 30 -- for about 34 per cent. Of course I have detailed information here, but this is an average figure. That is about 34 per cent. And the Catholics, the Roman Catholics in mid-nineteenth century, that is, prior to the occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for about 14 to 15 per cent. During the Austro-Hungarian occupation, that is, between the 1878 to the First World War, it changed. There were 43, 44 per cent of the Orthodox population; the number of Muslims dropped from 36 to 32, owing to a part to the immigration of Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina following the Austro-Hungarian occupation in '78. And the number of Catholics increased and in 1910 was about 22 per cent. Between the two world wars, and there were no major changes in the population structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, Orthodox Serbs, totalled 43, 44 per cent; the Muslims around 32 per cent; and the Roman Catholics around 21, 22 per cent. More substantive changes in the structure of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina started as of the 1970s, due largely to the political developments in the former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. As result of the disintegration of the Yugoslav state and as a result of its accelerating disintegration in the '70s and '80s --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, my apologies. In the '70s of the 20th century, it says 1970s, and it is 1970s. I'm sure that you can give us a detailed answer to this question, but we have limited time. Can you tell us what the situation is now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: It is very important. If one is to understand what happened towards the end of the twentieth century, and so that is why. And I'm talking about demographic losses. I'm talking about the demographic losses of the Bosnian-Herzegovinan population, primarily of the Serb population, because that decline was so drastic that it led to collective traumas. According to the research of our historians, our scientists and especially Professor Milorad Ekmecic, in the First World War, 19 per cent of the Bosnian population perished in World War II, and -- World War I. Such -- the first concentration camps were set up for Serbs in World War I. 25 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina perished in World War II. So these are horrible data. These are losses -- these huge demographic losses conduced to the fact that the Serbs in the struggle to create their ethnic state, just like Germans and other European peoples, and in the struggle to defend their own state, following all these horrible, horrific experiences. The loss of the state that they lived in, the former Yugoslavia, has resulted in terrible traumas and frustrations, and that is why they wanted to continue living in that federal state of Yugoslavia, fearing that in any other state they could experience once again the horrendous crimes that they experienced in the First and Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Terzic. Witness, from the contents of your answer and the contents of your statement, one can conclude that you think that the policy of the big powers affected fatefully the developments in the Balkans and the establishment of national boundaries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately it is correct, and I am the advocate of the principle, and it is -- when it is frequently said that Balkanism is synonymous for tribal strife. I think that Balkanism is -- epitomises tribal strife in the world today but the chief culprit for this is the policy of the big powers towards the Balkans because the big powers formed national liberation movements in the Balkans, not on the basis of principles that govern such movements in Germany, Italy, or perhaps other parts of Europe, but depending on their own interest and therefore they drew the boundaries of states in line with their strategic interest in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies, witness, but I have just one short question: Such a policy that as you deem it, did it also find it reflection in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: It found its reflection primarily in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is something ironic. There is a paradox. In 1907, the Bosnian-Herzegovinan Serbs and Muslims, there were 71 signatures, including three Muslim. In 1907, they sent a memorandum to the international conference on peace in -- in the international peace conference in The Hague in 1907 requesting that an end be put to the Austro-Hungarian occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because that occupation had failed. And just one more sentence. There are some historians - and I'm one of the partisans of such views - that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina 1992-1995 started in point of fact in 1878, when tens of thousands of Austro-Hungarian soldiers occupied by force Bosnia-Herzegovina, following the mandate of the Berlin Congress. And right up to the 1918, that is, until the creation of the Yugoslav state, Austria-Hungary manipulated ethnic, racial, religious hatreds and passions and the hatred that we find dates back to the days of the Austro-Hungarian policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Ms. Mahindaratne, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. You'll now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, Dr. Terzic. Cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Terzic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your report is titled "On the past of Bosnia-Herzegovina with special emphasis on Sarajevo." The title doesn't make specific reference to any of the ethnic communities which lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Sarajevo, at the beginning of the conflict. Did you intend your report to be a review of the history of all of these ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That was my duty. And I tried to supply the information about the history of the Serb people and history of Muslims and history of Croats, of course, depending on their number and their share in the development of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since the Serbs were the most populous group and since they were the ones who made the biggest contribution to the development of Bosnia-Herzegovina Sarajevo, and especially the modernisation of the Sarajevo society, I paid more attention to Serbs. But I also spoke about Muslims, perhaps a little less about Catholic Croats because their share in the Bosnian population was about 14, 15 per cent. But at any rate, I wanted to divide my attention equitably between the Serb, Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Terzic, your speed of speech is such that if you will slow down, it will be easier for the interpreters, a bit of breath now and then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you intend it to be an impartial and objective history in respect of these communities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is every historian's duty to speak sine ira et studio, that is, without wrath or bias, as the Roman proverb says. So I endeavoured, I tried hard not to be partial. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that your report in fact reads as a sympathetic history of the Bosnian Serb community in Bosnia and Herzegovina to the almost total exclusion of other communities. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Well, I will not comment on your impression, but that is precisely what I'm trying to say, that all European scientists in the nineteenth century thought that Bosnia-Herzegovina was Serb land. I could quote about ten eminent European historians, in the first place the most prominent German historian of the nineteenth century, Leopold von Ranke. In his work, "the Serb Revolution," published in 1829, and in his second work, "Turkey and Serbia," Leopold von Ranke, considers that Bosnia-Herzegovina are Serb lands. And this opinion is shared by many other researchers such as Ami Boue, a Russian traveller and diplomat Alexander Guilferding, and a number of British and other researchers. And this fact is further corroborated, among other things, by the London Pact of August 1915, when the big powers, that is, Great Britain, France, and Italy, decided to, within the framework following World War I, in case of the Allies victory, the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be integrated in the Serb national state. Sir Edward Gray pointed out in particular that that principle would be governed by the principle of the equality of nationalities. My view, or rather, the view that you have gained, can be justified because the sciences and such, and I mentioned only some of the names, considered Bosnia-Herzegovina as populated by the majority Serb population and that the Muslim population living there was also in terms of its origin of the Islamic, that is, of the Serb origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I'm not in the English booth, but in the B/C/S booth, I have some difficulties following the questions of my learned friend. But formally I think one should be able to read it in the transcript, but one does not see this text in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There were some problems related to the speed of speech, not only for the interpreters but also for the transcribers. And where the transcript reads: Kindly slow down for the purposes of the record," I think the question interrupted was that "I suggest to you that the report in fact reads as a --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sympathetic history, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sympathetic history of the Bosnian-Herzegovinan community in ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that was the question. This is just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's Bosnian Serb community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb community in Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes. This was just for the record, Dr. Terzic, so you don't have to pay attention -- you don't have to answer that question again. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask -- you have a very high speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that historically speaking it is more correct and in literature it is -- the term usually used is the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather than the Bosnian Serb community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the clarification. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Terzic, under chapter 9 of the Table of Contents, there are several sections under which you report on Bosnian Serb institutions, areas of activity, and important historical events. For instance, the first section deals with Serbs in the urban culture of Sarajevo and their contribution to the multicultural environment. Now, where in your report can one find a similar consideration by you of the achievements and contribution of the Bosnian Croat community or those of the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: In parts concerning life under Austro-Hungarian occupation between 1878 to 1918, I also paid attention to institutions set up by Muslims and Roman Catholics. And you will find in several places, find examples of newspapers or institutions published or organised by Muslims. For instance, magazines, journals. I indicated Bosansko-Hercegovacki Glasnik edited by Omer Bey Sulejman-Pasic or Samouprava, by Osman Djikic, then an organ of Muslim dissidence and so on and so forth, that this -- as far as the written press is concerned. I also mentioned some Croat cultural institutions and some of their business institutions. For instance, when we talk about Bosansko-Hercegovacka Narodna Dionicka Banka founded in 1878, I indicated that of 17 founders, in addition to Muslims and Jews, there were also seven Serbs. And I also, when it comes to political circumstances following the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1910, I also indicated that in addition to Serb -- three Serb members of parliament in Sarajevo, I also indicated four Muslims from Sarajevo who were also members of parliament and one Croat who was elected by the Croat cooperative, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, chapter 9 -- under chapter 9, you have several sections which include Serb institutions, Serb activity, and important historical events relating to the Serb community. Now, you have specifically dealt with -- dealt under separate sections, under the titles of Serb institutions or relating to Serb events and activity. Now, why is it that you have focussed on the -- these aspects relating to the Serbian community and excluded achievements and contributions and institutions relating to the other two principal communities? Why have you focussed only on the Serbian communities, activities, and institutions, if your report was to be submitted in the context of impartiality and objectivity?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, I studied in particular the role of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in view of the nature of this case and this hearing. But on no occasion did I want to ignore, to neglect, either Muslims or Croats. However, the share of Muslims and Croats in the development of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not the same as the role of the Serbs, Orthodox Serbs in the first place, simply because in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were 14 to 17 per cent of Croats and that there were about 32 per cent of Muslims and that there were about 44 per cent of Serbs. When we speak about the building of a modern European society, that is, the creation of commercial institutions, banks, educational establishments, literary magazines, cultural societies, then Serbs, Orthodox Serbs have left a major mark in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is because that is how it was in the past. And I wanted to show that, trying to avoid any false symmetry regarding the roles and parts of different peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I wanted to present things as they truly were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Your report in the Serbian version is 44 pages in length. Only approximately five pages --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only approximately five pages, and mainly the last two pages, deal with events concerning Sarajevo from 1981. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to the overall history of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that part, that is, the '90s, the modern part, is somewhat shorter than the previous epochs, and I can explain why. If I may, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, sir. In the interest of time, that won't be necessary. Drawing your attention to page 33 of your report - and I'm referring to the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before you continue, the witness addressed me, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you would agree that the part of the recent Sarajevan history would be far shorter than the other part. If you ask whether the witness agrees, it has some meaning. So if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the witness wants to explain, he should be given at least a short opportunity to do so, unless in your questions to come you'll ask for such an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't intent to ask him for any further explanations on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if a historian writes a report and if --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Only A small part relates to the more recent history of the area of Sarajevo, and if you ask him whether he agrees that it's a very small portion, then he should be allowed to explain why it was such a small portion. So please explain why you wrote on the smaller portion of your wrote on Sarajevo in the '90s, but please keep your explanation concise because the parties are under some time constraint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Obviously, we approach this problem from different angles. I described 1990s in general outlines. As a historian, I think regardless of this Tribunal's activity, that we still do not have - I mean, as historians - relevant historical material which would allow us to establish full historical truths. There is a major methodological problem there, and we cannot establish the historical truth on the basis of printed media or personal reminisces, because these are third-rate sources. We lack crucial archival information, we lack the records of secret negotiations, we have no access to special services, secret services, we do not have access to the sittings of any governments or deliberations of any governments, and this will become accessible only in the future. Only then will historians be able to objectively consider the events in Bosnia at that time, so that we can make our judgments on the basis of what we have, and that is very little, because we lack crucial documents. And I believe that some day, when my colleagues write the history of these developments, their picture will be quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you to be concise. I do understand your question to be that the sources for the recent history are not fully accessible yet and that it would be difficult to write a full history of the 1990s in Sarajevo. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, a substantial part of your report, some seven pages in the B/C/S version and nine pages in English, deals with persecution in one form or another of Sarajevo Serbs during World War I, and that is 1914 to 1918. How, if at all, do you think an understanding of the history of the treatment of the Serbian community during World War I contributes to an understanding of the events in Sarajevo between 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Madam, I think this is a very important question, and I'm sorry if you are unable to understand the outstanding importance of this question. The political conduct of people, their world is also made of historical reminiscences and memories and experience and traumas. In the 1990s, there were still a lot of people whose fathers had perished en masse in the concentration camps in World War I. During World War I in Bosnia-Herzegovina, over 100.000 children under the age of 14 died, and this was a terrible ordeal which has left a deep imprint in the soul and the tradition of the Serb people. Somebody may think it very remote, but for a human life-span that is not remote, and it all happened in an even worse way in World War II, it was even more horrendous, so that I think that the fact about the ordeal of Serbs in World War I, via concentration camps, mass exterminations, a large number of political processes -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina during World War I there were dozens of political processes trying Serbs only. The biggest one took place in Banja Luka in 1915-1916, when 156 Serbs were tried and sentenced. The entire Serb intelligentsia of Bosnia-Herzegovina, teachers MPs, priests, peasants, and the chief charge was an inspiration to create a greater Serbia. I, therefore, think this is very important because that experience from the first big war largely conduced to a major trauma of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that this traumatic and powerful history was capable of motivating some members of the Bosnian Serb community in 1992 and thereafter to go to extreme lengths to secure their autonomous independence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: That factor was of great importance, the factor from the First World War, and particularly the experience of the Second World War. This caused panic to appear, panic relating to the loss of one's own state, because a crime in the First World War and a crime in the Second World War -- in the First World War it was under the Austro-Hungarian authorities, and in the Second World War they were carried out during the Ustasha reign. The fear remained that in someone else's state such a genocide could be committed, and this was the key reason for the historical and psychological behaviour of the Serbs in the 1990s. Mr. President, I would like to add that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's addition: The witness mentioned crimes being committed during the Second World War under the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to add something, and you waited for Ms. Mahindaratne to, having terminated this -- her consultation. What would you like to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My attention was drawn to the First World War. I would like to draw your attention to the Second World War. That was a terrible experience. I would like to quote German sources here. Hitler's official for the south-eastern in autumn 1943, Hermann Neubacher, in his diary, which was published in Gottingen in 1958, he says that the crimes committed against the Serbs in the independent state of Croatia, and I quote, "were the worst mass murders committed in the course of history," and I'm quoting Neubacher. He considers that in the course of the Second World War about 750.000 Serbs were killed in the independent state of Croatia. Another German, Alexander von Lohr, commander in the south-east, says that from April 1941 until the autumn of 1942 about 400.000 Serbs were killed in the independent state of Croatia. The number of Serbs killed in the course of the Second World War in the independent state of Croatia is between 800.000 and 1 million people. This includes tens of thousands of children. After such a terrible genocide, there is not a single family that was not marked by this and traumatised by this. This was all fresh for many people. Many people were born in camps. Many people were born when they were refugees and they participated in the events at the end of the twentieth century. So to have an objective understanding of the events that occurred in the 1990s, I think that is extremely important to bear in mind the general historical and political and psychological contexts which motivated people to act in certain ways. This is very important. So the Serbs were afraid that in the 1990s and in someone else's states, in Bosnia and Herzegovina or in Croatia, the genocide committed in the First and Second World War would be repeated. This is what they were afraid of. And this was one of the important political reasons for their activities. After the disintegration of Yugoslavia, they wanted to live together with the other Serbian population, that is to say, together with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, moving on to a different area. I draw your attention to page 49 of your report, the English version. On the fourth line, you state -- I will read it to you, "The clause stipulating that parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina by self-determination of two-thirds of the population at a referendum may secede and join the neighbouring republics was deleted." Now, what is the constitutional provision in the 1974 constitution, which you're referring to here, as having been deleted by an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. amendment in 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Madam, I'm referring to Article 5 of the constitution of 1974, which states, and I quote: Article 5 of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1974, and I quote: "The territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is comprised of the territory of municipalities. The territory, that is to say, the borders of the republics can be changed by a decision of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and only in accordance with the expressed wish of the population of a certain area and in accordance with the general interests of the republic and on the basis of an agreement with the neighbouring republic." That is what Article 5 states.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have copies of that particular article. May I just distribute it for the purpose of cross-examination from here on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have it in B/C/S, as well as in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do not intend to tender it, but just for reference during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position that you interpret Article 5 as a constitutional basis for secession by majority of two-thirds at a referendum? Is that how you interpret that article?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I am not a lawyer, first of all, but I think I can interpret this article and interpret what it says. And that means that the constitution from 1974 allowed for the possibility, in the case of certain regions or areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it states here, it allowed for the possibility that they should join a different republic with agreement of that republic and with the agreement of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have read that article, and I don't think that it's a matter of secession because they are discussing one state. You are forgetting one thing, madam: One state is concerned here, which is called the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Republics are part of this federal state. In the amendment 99, Article 7, from 1990, so after the amendments to the constitution of 1974, it was forbidden there for -- to politically get organised and to act in order to threaten the territorial integrity of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So this was in agreement with the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So it had to do with the fact that parts of the republic could join another republic if this was what the population wanted and those two republics desired this, and they could do this within the framework of one state, the Federal State of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on a plain reading of Article 5, isn't it clear that the provision allows for the adjustment of the borders which is far from secession [Realtime transcript read in error "cessation"] and joining the border republics, which is what you have claimed in page 49 of your report in line 4?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I am only saying what it states in Article 5, and I would like to read it out again so that I don't interpret it. It also says that the territory, or rather, "the borders of republics can be changed by a decision of the assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, only in agreement with the expressed desire of the population from the relevant area and in accordance with the general interests of the republic and on the basis of an agreement with neighbouring republics." So we are dealing with the possible changes to the borders of a republic within the framework of an internationally recognised state, and that is the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And let me say this: The borders of republics are administrative. They aren't internationally recognised, if the great powers haven't recognised them. And I would also like to take advantage of this opportunity to say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm just a little confused. I wanted to verify whether we -- my learned friend is talking about cessation or secession. This does not mean the same thing. The question in English had to the with cessation, and I think that we are discussing another issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you meant secession.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And not cessation. Yes, as a not native English speaker myself, I know how difficult it is to pronounce the word in such a way that confusion is avoided. I take it that there has been no misunderstanding, also for the booth, that Ms. Mahindaratne was talking about secession, rather than cessation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You're correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. Is this the time for a break or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I at the same time ask you how much time you'd still approximately need, taking into account that you used approximately some -- a little bit over 30 minutes until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps at the most another 15, 20 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the time scheduled was 45 minutes, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: One hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour, yes. I'm always trying to cut down, Ms. Mahindaratne. We'll adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought in the courtroom. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, going back to the issue of that sentence on page 49, line 4, you referred to an amendment adopted in 1990 as having deleted the clause you referred to, that is, Article 5. Now, which amendment are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I didn't carry out a legal analysis of this process. What was important for me was the fact that the constitutional amendments from the 1990s introduced certain amendments with regard to the constitution of 1974. And what was especially important for me was the change in Amendment 69, item 7 and 10. So the changes in the constitution of 1974, in Amendment 69, item 7, from 1990, it states that "It is prohibited to carry out political organisation and activities which threaten the integrity of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. I'm referring to the amendment which replaced Article 5, which you referred to in page 49, the English version of the report. Was it Amendment number 62 that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: No, it's 1772 in which Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, the fact that it is a sovereign and integral part of the Yugoslav community is emphasised. This is in Amendment 1772. But I wanted to draw your attention to item 10 of Amendment 69, which introduced significant changes in relation to the constitution of 1974, and that is to say that in Amendment 69, item 10, a council for issues of obtaining equality between peoples and nationalities was formed, and it had 20 members from each national group and not a single matter of importance for the destiny of the republic, for the fate of the republic could be decided on without the agreement of all the peoples, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims, in agreement with --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I may interrupt you. In the sentence I'm referring to, you referred to a two-thirds majority vote at a referendum. Now, from where in Article 5 did you derive that changes to the borders of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. territory could be made with a two-thirds majority obtained at a referendum? Now, where in Article 5 did you obtain that aspect?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Madam, you're thinking of Article 5 of the constitution from 1974.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: In that article -- I didn't even claim that it mentioned a two-thirds majority in that article. Please, listen to me carefully. I'll read out Article 5 once more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. I'm going back to your report. I will read line 4 of page 49, and this is your report. You state: "The clause stipulating that parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by self-determination of two-thirds of population at a referendum may secede and join the neighbouring republics --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And join the neighbouring republics was deleted." Now, in referring to the word "clause," you're referring to a provision in the 1974 constitution. And when I questioned you as to which provision you were referring to, you said Article 5. Now, my question is: From where in Article 5 did you derive the aspect of a two-thirds majority and a referendum? It's your assertion that I'm putting back to you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, madam. You're saying something I didn't state. I didn't say that in Article 5 there was a provision on two-thirds majority. I read the entire Article 5 out, and I would like to do so again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let me just interfere. There seems to be some confusion. Ms. Mahindaratne is referring to a part of your report and she has put some questions to you, but it seems that it is her problem now, where does she find the two-third majority in a referendum that would be needed for self-determination, because you, I think, on a question you answered, it was in Article 5, but it seems to be not what you intend to express. So where can she find the requirement of two-third majority?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my position was that in line 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, she can find it in Amendment number 69, the amendment of the constitution of 1974. It's from 1999, and it's item 10. And they mention the council of realising equality between peoples and nationalities in which there will be 20 representatives for each people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just finish, please. If at least 20 deputies, 20 members of that council consider that a certain people is not equal, in that case the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall follow a special procedure provided for in the rules and the decision will be taken on the basis of a two-thirds majority. It's item 10, Amendment 69, and the year is 1999. So this means that a referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina should have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. My only question was where Ms. Mahindaratne could find the two-third majority, and I do understand from her that that was not quite her question. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in page 49, I will read this to you. Please correct me as to whether you've stated so in your report. You refer to the 1974 constitution and you go on to say: "The clause stipulating that parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by self-determination of the two-third of population at a referendum may secede and join the neighbouring republics, was deleted." And from that I understand that you referred to a constitutional provision in the 1974 constitution which provided for secession by a two-thirds majority vote at a referendum was deleted by an amendment in 1990. Now, was that what you intended to say, because that is how it has been written in your report.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that in Article 5 from the 1990s it was possible to change the borders of the republics within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia if the population from certain regions expressed this wish and with the agreement of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the agreement of neighbouring republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, in that sentence, you referred to the possibility of such changes being effected by means of a referendum whereby you have to obtain a two-thirds majority vote. You mentioned that aspect in that sentence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying that in accordance with Article 5, in accordance with the expressed desire of the population of a given area, this was checked through a referendum or plebiscite, the desire, the wishes of the population was checked in this way. This was the customary procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you was: Where in Article 5 of the 1974 constitution, prior to amendment, was there a provision for border changes to be effected by a two-thirds majority at a referendum? From where did you derive that term "two-thirds majority" at a referendum from Article 5?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: In Article 5, it does not explicitly say two-thirds majority, but it says that the territory can be changed only in keeping with the will of the people of a particular republic, and it is basically understood that this will be established by referendum and it was customary to have a two-thirds majority to make such a decision final.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going to ask a question to the witness. The same page, 49 of the English report. At the end of the same paragraph, it says the following: "Yet the constitutional provision on the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not respected, which prescribes that the status can be changed only with the majority of two-thirds of votes at a general people's referendum." You mention a constitutional provision there, not a customary law but a constitutional provision. Which is that constitutional provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the provision in the Amendment 69, item 10, to the constitution -- adopted in 1990 to the constitution of 1974. And I will repeat once again: It has to do with the council for the equality of nations and nationalities which says that if an ethnic community objects to a particular problem, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall decide on the matter by two-thirds majority of the total number of votes. So it is Article 69, item 10 of the amendments of 1990. This meant, in other words, that in a referendum for independence of the 29th of February and the 1st of March, to make its decision final, 66.6 per cent of the overall electorate of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to vote for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So it is an amendment made in 1990. It's not in the constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right. Amendment 69, item 10 was adopted in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the same page, in the same paragraph, fourth line from the bottom of that paragraph, you state that "The referendum results were not officially published." What was the basis for you to claim that referendum results were not officially published?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: First, I said it on the basis of a casual words with the president of the party. Democratic action, Alija Izetbegovic, who immediately following the referendum said that almost 63 per cent of voters voted in the referendum, and I said it on the basis of Noel Malcolm's book, "Bosnia, a brief history," in which he says on page 231 that, and I quote, "About 64 per cent of --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last word. 64 per cent of ... We could not hear what he said last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please repeat where you said "about 64 per cent of" what? Because the interpreters could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Noel Malcolm, the author of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. book, "Bosnia, a brief history," speaks about the results of the referendum for independence and says that this was, I quote, "An about 64 per cent victory." Page 231 in Noel Malcolm. For the referendum to succeed, one needed 66.6 per cent of votes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why does that lead you to conclude that the referendum results were not officially published?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Because the author of the book says that, Noel Malcolm, he says "about 64 per cent." If he says "about" or "approximately," it means that this is not exact, that he does not have a reliable source. So that is one thing. And secondly, that percentage which he quotes, 64 per cent approximately, is not the same as 66.6, which is the only result which could make the upshot of the referendum valid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Terzic, may I ask you to listen very carefully to the questions and answer specifically to the questions, because you were asked: What does lead you to conclude that the referendum results were not officially published? That was the question. Your answer was about the results of the referendum but not specifically what made you conclude that they were not officially published. So the question is: Is there an official publication? If not, what makes you believe that there was no official publication. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat it once again. I was driven to that conclusion by the conclusion of my colleague Noel Malcolm in his book "Bosnian, a brief history," in which he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat your answer. If you say there is no official publication since the only source from which I can learn the result is a book published by Mr. X, Y, or Z, that's an answer to the question, I would take it, and you are not yet asked to comment on the content of the book. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown a document, if I may have the assistance of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We have sufficient copies -- we have sufficient copies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the text be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you -- if there is one copy available, could you please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I thought there were sufficient copies distributed to the interpreters. It was distributed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If not, I have an extra copy available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please take care that extra copies are distributed for the booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We have some more copies here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what this document is? Could you please read the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Which page do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the top of the page - it is page 200 - you will see there's a title to this page.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: "The Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: 27th March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you note on the second page, attached to this document, that is, page number 201, there is an official announcement of the referendum results published there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But I notice what I just said. And if I may, I will quote it. Of the total number of voters, 3.253.847 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. Therefore, do you now concede that you made a mistake with regard to your position that referendum results were not officially published? It is incorrect, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: No. At that moment in time, I was not familiar with the official results. But this is less important than the chief fact that I'm putting to you, and that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Terzic, it's not for you at this moment to decide what is of importance. Ms. Mahindaratne questions you about the part of your report where it says that the results were never officially published. That's the point she wants to deal with at this very moment. And she now asks you whether you agree that this document indicates that the results were officially published.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that in this text I did not use the results from the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I used the results from Noel Malcolm's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did write that they were never officially published, isn't it? That's the issue, not on whether this is a correct publication or whether someone else correctly published it. The issue Ms. Mahindaratne raises is that you write that they were never officially published, and I take it that she wants to establish that you made a mistake in respect of the fact that they were officially published. That's what she asks you. That's the issue at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. No. That is, I didn't write that they were never officially published. I never wrote that they had never been officially published, but that at that moment they were not published yet. But as one sees from this Official Gazette, they were published almost a month later. So I didn't say and my text doesn't say they were never officially published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you write your report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: I wrote the report in 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this official publication is -- was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But I was explaining the situation related to the referendum. I was explaining that in the wake of the referendum, there were no official results but that they were published a month later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to deal with a whole area, Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same page in the second paragraph, line 6 -- I beg your pardon, line 5, you go on to say: "The United States of America and the European Community threatened by an ultimatum that the JNA should withdraw." Now, what was the ultimatum that you referred to here? What did the United States and the European Community threaten would happen if the JNA did not withdraw?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: These are common facts. We've all read about it many times. I think that the US state secretary, Henry Kissinger was quite right when in an interview to La Stampa of the 21st of February 1993 said, and I quote, "the most irresponsible mistake which caused the tragedy was committed when the Bosnian state under the Muslim government of Alija Izetbegovic were internationally recognised." So after the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again have to remind you that a question is put to you. You should listen to the question and you should give an answer to the question. Whether it was a fatal mistake by whomever to do whatever was not the question. The question was: What did the United States and the European Community threaten would happen if the JNA did not withdraw? That's the question. Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Of course. Well, they issued threats every day. And the pressure was such that when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is what did they threaten? If you say it was a general threat, fine. Explain then. Or you will ask to explain. Or if you say it was a repeated threat, fine. But the question is: What did they threaten with? What would happen if there would be no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sanctions would happen against the remainder of Yugoslavia, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And that finally did happen in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question again -- your answer is now clear: They threatened with sanctions. If Ms. Mahindaratne would like to know what sanctions, she'll certainly ask you and she also whether it's true or not and whether they put any sanctions is a different matter. Please listen to the questions and answer to the questions. Yes? Yes. So the answer is that they threatened with sanctions, Ms. Mahindaratne. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
