utterances.text: Sir, isn't it the case that it was the UN Security Council that demanded for withdrawal and not the United States or the European Community? The issue of sanctions come in the context of the demand for withdrawal made by the UN Security Council; isn't it the case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: The Security Council was but a tool in the hands of the politicians of the United States of America and the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Is there any need to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you, since the other Judges have no questions. I'm putting a question to you in relation to your last answer. You said that the Security Council was the tool in the hands of the politicians of the United States of America and the European Union. Is it your view that the United Nations -- the United States and the European Union could impose their will on the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I'm quite confident that that is so. The course of events over the past 10, 20 years shows that unfortunately the Security Council has become a tool in the -- a tool in the hands of the United States and some European states, unfortunately. This secession and the recognition of a secession in the Socialist Republic of the Republic of Yugoslavia was a precedent in international law. We see that at the end of the twentieth century, we found ourselves with a completely warped system of international law because unfortunately the big powers have been pursuing a completely irresponsible policy, which then resulted in a very bloody tragedy in the Yugoslav lands. Speaking as a historian, bearing in mind the nineteenth century, when on the European stage there were a number of wise politicians, great men, and fantastic diplomats at the end of the twentieth century, on the political stage of Europe and the world, there were a number of mediocre people, people who were not up to the task. They started problems, they opened problems without knowing how to solve them. We now have a crisis which is lasting, and I'm not sure that it will be resolved in the conceivable future, and that unfortunately is a tragic fact. Let us take for instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the use of right of veto by any of the other permanent members of the Security Council, would that not have stopped the United States and the European Union members? I mean, all the permanent members can say no to resolutions; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. And I am not a diplomat. But if I may make a forecast, I believe that in apart from the Wiesner [phoen] principle, it would have taken place. Unfortunately the untimely - untimely - recognition of secession of Yugoslav republics before a political understanding was reached within the Yugoslav state is what led to that great tragedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was not an answer to my question. My question was that if there are three permanent members belonging to the group you just mentioned, that there are two permanent members of the Security Council not being part of the group of states you just mentioned. And since it sounds as if you're blaming the United States and the European Union, I wondered what your view was on the other states not using their veto power.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your question, Mr. President, is quite logical. I suppose you mean China or Russia. But it was proven once again on that occasion that big powers, in pursuit of their own interests, will often sacrifice the interests of small peoples, and that is one of the tragic lessons of history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That certainly is an answer to my question. Dr. Terzic, assuming that the questions of the Bench have not raised any issue, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I merely wish to make something precise. The witness has just said "if you mean China and USSR," rather than China or USSR, as the transcript says. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it would make a great distinction, because voting you do alone and not together. The veto power is on each of the permanent members. Dr. Terzic, this then concludes your testimony in this court. You have answered only a limited number of questions from the Defence, but they have presented your report, which we have read carefully. You have answered the questions put by both parties and by the Bench to you. I thank you very much for coming, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. About the book. Perhaps I should have responded. It's not usual, Dr. Terzic, that a Chamber trying a case accepts presents. But I am -- the Chamber, of course, highly appreciates that you want to provide us with as much information as possible. And if I'm not misinformed, the library of this Tribunal has accepted in the past presents from those who want to contribute to the work of the Tribunal by giving books. That would then, of course, not be the Trial Chamber but that is -- I don't know whether a special regulation for accepting presents, but I think that would be the appropriate place to address. And I can tell you that we have many books. I don't know whether this one is already in there or not. Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Dr. Terzic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I meant. For the library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- if you take it and ask the Victims and Witnesses Unit whether they can pave you the way to the library and see whether any regulations in force for the acceptance of -- but we highly appreciate your offer as such, but as a Trial Chamber of course we cannot accept. It's the parties here who introduce material that is in evidence and that the Chamber will consider. Thank you very much. I don't know. You missed part of the explanation. I said it is up to the parties to provide material to the Court, and sometimes they do provide part of books as well. Yes? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to raise an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are several annexes to this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Most of which are in B/C/S, B/C/S or Russian, Mr. President. And we have made repeated requests to the Defence to provide us with English translations of these annexes, which have not been complied with to date. In view of that, Mr. President, the Prosecution moves that those annexes be withdrawn from evidence for the reason, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. President, the Prosecution has not had the opportunity to read these -- peruse these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But my impression is that my colleagues now make their request when it comes to Dr. Slavenko Terzic's expert opinion. We had several meetings, and at one of those meetings specifically, Ms. Mahindaratne was present, but the only request made for Dr. Terzic's cv, rather than copies of annexes accompanying the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not the case. In fact, at that very meeting the Prosecution requested for all annexes to both reports of Dr. Terzic as well as annexes to Dr. Guskova, as well as there is a motion in writing where we have requested for these documents, English translations of these documents, which was filed a couple of weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. I also remember that when we discussed the motion in this courtroom, I think that the parties did offer each other assistance, in this case the Defence offered assistance in order to receive translated copies of these documents. I haven't got all the details in my mind, whether it was more in general terms or specifically on the report of Dr. Terzic. Ms. Pilipovic, the request of the Prosecution is that you withdraw. I take it from your answer that you would rather not withdraw these documents as annexes to the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first time that the Prosecution has made this request. At the meeting that we had, I think a month and a half ago, a request was made for the translation of the footnotes accompanying Mrs. Guskova's reports. We provided the translation of the footnotes in time for the annexes, and in particular for Dr. Terzic's report no such requests were made. I'll try and find the request. I'll check. But I don't think that we have received such requests for this report to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I was present at the meeting, and sadly this is the difficulty that arises when we have meetings off the record. It may prompt the memory of my learned colleagues, it may not. The Prosecution at that meeting requested translations into an official language of the UN. Mr. Piletta-Zanin was present as well. He said he was going to Geneva in the next few days and he would make some inquiries as to whether he had the translation resources there to do it. We heard nothing further from the Defence as to the translation of the annexes but we did then receive a translation of the footnotes, and that was the last communication with the Defence outside court on the issue. In the meantime or earlier, we had formally raised it, and I think there was an understanding that -- perhaps a suggestion from the Trial Chamber that the parties should try and resolve it, when Mrs. Pilipovic said in court that she was happy to talk to us. And that's as far as it went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber is not present during such meetings. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would like to add, because we started with Ms. Mahindaratne, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Ierace was during the meeting present. And I now hear that you were present as well. So you're the fourth in a row to inform us about it. And please, if you could briefly explain your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, gladly. Mr. Ierace is absolutely right. He's right when he says that I was there, and that's the extent to which he has right, because this meeting with Mr. Ierace, what I said there is as follows: With regard to the Russian expert that we are mentioning, the doctor that we heard, I told Mr. Ierace in his mother tongue the following: It was at the end of the week. I said I'm going to return to Geneva soon. I'm going to see if I can find some translators there. And if that's the case, you'll be informed of this immediately, next week. Naturally I didn't want to bother Mr. Ierace to tell him that I hadn't found anyone. Mr. Ierace can understand quite well that if a translation had been found, someone to translate from Russian to English or from French, I would have -- I didn't provide him with an answer about this immediately because I wasn't able to. If Mr. Ierace can't understand this, well, on each occasion it will be necessary for us to write this out, and we'll lose a lot of time. So yes, I was there. My position was stated in relation to the expert Guskova and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... On details of what has been said stands, details that are not without relevance for the issue raised. One thing is for sure: No member of this Chamber is able to read any B/C/S document. So whatever is valid for the preparation of cross-examination certainly we will not be able to read any document that is not translated in either English or French. I would suggest to the parties that they seek in whatever way a compromise on this issue. If not, the Chamber will decide. Then that was your issue you wanted to raise, Ms. Mahindaratne. Is there any document one of the parties would want to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Those documents were just merely used for the purpose of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Used for the purpose. Then I should inform the parties that we dealt with the documents tendered by the parties in respect of the testimony of Dr. Vilicic. The Chamber would like to have some more documents in evidence as those tendered by the parties. I think not all the tables are admitted, especially not the tables produced by Professor Vilicic himself. We'll deal with that tomorrow when we have a full list of what the Chamber would like to have in evidence, and whether we call it then that the parties are ordered to produce that or that is evidence which the Chamber calls. We'll deal with that tomorrow. It would take too much time at this very moment. I'm specifically referring to all kind of tables and sketches. Having dealt with that, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the usher could escort the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Might I be excused, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are excused, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I take it that you are Dr. Kuljic? Dr. Kuljic, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. First of all, good day to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Kuljic. Please be seated. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is it you or is it Ms. Pilipovic who is going to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, could you briefly introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber and can you tell us what your professional and scientific background is, in a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: I am a doctor of medicine, a specialist in psychiatry, also a master of science and a doctor of medical science. I work in the institution for mental health and I work there as the clinic coordinator. I'm involved in the work of a psychiatrist. As far as my scientific experience, my scientific background is concerned to date, I've participated in several articles which were presented at international congresses and these articles have also been published in magazines. My masters and Ph.D. degree dealt with the subject of stress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what the title of your thesis, your Ph.D. thesis is.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: The title was "Risk factors in developing acute stress symptoms after being wounded."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Doctor, if you could just answer by saying yes or no, I would appreciate that. In the course of your work and in relation to your thesis, did you have the opportunity of elaborating scientific questionnaires -- have you had the opportunity of taking samples, population samples? Have you had the opportunity of carrying out such work?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, we are now going to turn to your work. On the 14th of January, 2002 you provided an opinion expert, an expert report that I have in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, one of the usual questions in the beginning of testimony of an expert witness is his name, date of birth, et cetera, so that we know for certain that the person I called Dr. Kuljic is -- perhaps we better do that at the beginning of the testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I hope that you'll forgive me for this unforgivable error on my part. Could you please tell me what your name is, your first name, your last name, and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: My first name is Blagoje, my last name is Kuljic. I was born on the 24th of April, 1966.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where? I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: I was born in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we have solved that matter. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And don't be too pessimistic that it will be unforgivable. I'm certain that it will be forgiven. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, on the 14th of January, 2003 you provided -- you submitted this report that I have in front of me. My question is as follows: Do you confirm the contents of the report? Do you stand by your statements? Is there anything you would like to modify, something you would like to add? I'm only referring to the document such as it is.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: I stand by everything that I stated, and I'll be glad to provide certain clarifications, if this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I would now like to focus on questions of methodology. And if I asked you -- if I addressed you as professor, I'm only anticipating what will happen in the future. I apologise again. Doctor, I would now like to focus on the issue of methodology. If you have to conduct research work which involves a certain number of people, if it's, in a certain manner, a statistical report, what are the methodological bases that must absolutely be respected?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Well, when conducting research of any kind, first of all it's necessary to know what we are researching, what we are investigating, what the phenomenon among the population is. We have to inform what is known about that in the available literature and on the basis of certain personal experiences and then it is necessary to clearly specify the elements we are investigating and the population involved, and then we have to make an adequate plan. This means that we have to foresee the possible errors. If we are investigating factor A, which has an effect on factor -- or phenomenon B, we have to be certain to the extent that this is possible whether this is the only factor that has an influence, has an effect on this phenomena, because sometimes you get certain results that could be ascribed to the phenomenon but aren't part of it. So you have to be careful when compiling, when making such a plan. I'll just provide you an example. The influence of sound and light was investigated, the influence of this on the productivity of employees. This work was carried out, but finally we concluded that there was no such influence on their work but their work was influenced because of the investigation itself. The people were aware of the fact that they were being investigated and because of the influence of the investigators, the way in which they worked was different from how they would have worked in other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Thank you. You could perhaps speak a little more slowly so that we can all follow you clearly. Thank you. Doctor, you mentioned a plan. We'll focus on that a little later. But could you provide us with some basic information about forming samples, what we call samples.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Well, when we're investigating a phenomenon on the basis of a certain sample, we have to be aware of the fact that in certain situations when you are investigating a large number of the population, it's not possible to take all those concerned into consideration. So we'll select a certain number of people and consider them to be a representative sample. There are two main rules: The sample must be sufficiently large, and it has to be a random sample. If these rules are not respected, errors result, or rather, the results that we obtained could be different from the actual situation among the population being investigated. There are certain forms that deal with the size of the basic population and deal with certain factors that are being investigated on that basis, so you determine the number of people who have to be included in the study, the number of respondents. When I say this is customary, I'm just talk in an approximate way. Don't take this as a rule. But it's between 1 and 5 per cent when we conduct investigations of certain segments of the population. It's necessary for that sample, for the sample used to be a random sample, and that means that as an investigator I can't decide that I'll select this respondent, this person or that person, because I want to do so. In such cases, I might be biased. Very often the investigator, when writing his report, might introduce something that might influence the final result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you for this answer. Could you now try to be -- to provide us with more specific answers, to expand on this answer, in relation to Sarajevo and in relation to problems related to the terror in Sarajevo; that is to say, how would one have had to proceed as far as methodology is concerned, at that level alone? Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, it's necessary to think about what we want to investigate in Sarajevo, whether as Mr. Turner said, we want to investigate the subject of terror in Sarajevo, among the population of Sarajevo. So there are several methodological issues that arise here. As far as obtaining this answer is concerned, we have to see which factors, which circumstances could have an influence on the appearance of fear. We have to carry out a cognitive process -- an analysis of the cognitive process in which fear is felt, we have to consider how we are going to know what level, what degree of fear is concerned; that is to say, we have to make comparisons in order to have a sort of system of reference. We have to take some other city where war is also being waged. We have to measure the degree of fear there and compare it to the degree of fear felt in Sarajevo. And only then can we come to the conclusion as to whether the degree of fear was the same or different, whether there was greater fear. In all investigations, when we come across factors that we are not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. familiar with, when we come across things that we are not familiar with, we first of all have to inform ourselves, we have to find some sort of reference values because something that was perhaps fear in Sarajevo, in wartime circumstances, someone might perceive this as a high degree of fear and other people might perceive it as a low degree of fear. I'll provide you with a vivid example. If, for example, an extraterrestrial who is 3 metres tall appears suddenly in this courtroom, we'll say, "Look how big this extraterrestrial is." Ten minutes later five of his relatives appear who are between 5 and 6 metres tall, and at that point the first extraterrestrial will not seem so tall to us. We'll think that he is short. So we have to be able -- we have to be in a position to compare him with someone. We have to have a system of reference. When selecting the people we are going to include in the investigation, the people we're going to use to see how they experienced fear, we have to take into consideration the size of these respondents. We have to take into consideration the basic characteristics that will also provide a picture of Sarajevo before the war, and this will have to do with the territory that we are investigating, the territory which -- where war is being waged, and we have to take into consideration the age, the professional structure of these people from that area. We also have to take into account the entire territory of Sarajevo, and we have to take a certain number of subjects from all the areas in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now focus on this geographical subject. I must admit that I am not familiar with extraterrestrials as you are, but I do use bicycles and I'm going to use an example. If we represent Sarajevo as a bicycle wheel, and you have the tire, which is the sort of frontal zone, and the spikes, which converge on the centre, where there is not as much fighting as on the front line - this is hypothesis - would the degree of terror along one of those spikes or along several of those spikes, according to the location of the population, what would the degree of fear be with regard to the people at the front? Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And this is what is at issue. That is why I said that it was necessary to take into account the entire territory of Sarajevo, because we're talking about all the citizens of Sarajevo. So the rule has to be respected here. We also have to take into account people who were closer to the front lines and we have to take into account people who were further removed from the front lines, because as I said, for the sample to be a representative one this is one of the conditions that has to be respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This knowledge of principles that you have, could you now apply it to the work of your colleague, Mr. Turner. My question is as follows: Do you have a detailed knowledge of Mr. Turner's report? Did you have the possibility of reading it from beginning to end with the annexes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, could you now answer my question: What can you tell us about the methodology used in Mr. Turner's report and in relation to the samples used and the respect of the principles that you mentioned or failure to respect such principles?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: In the written version of my report, I provided explanations of this question. I'll try and be brief. The random nature of the sample was not a principle that was accepted. The criteria of the Prosecution were applied, and on the basis of those statements the expert arrived at his conclusions. Similarly, the structure, the gender structure, the age structure of the population, the educational background of the population, these factors must also be taken into account and then when interviewing -- when questioning witnesses at the court, at the Tribunal, and then if a psychiatrist comes to conclusions on the basis of such testimonies, the psychiatrist doesn't have adequate tools. It's like a surgeon who doesn't have the necessary tools to carry out his work. So psychiatric tests were not used, tests that would enable us to quantify the level of fear in question. Likewise, there were no psychiatric interviews which would have made it possible to establish with greater precision what one tries to establish in tests. Although, I have already said that an interview is more reliable, a psychiatrist interview - I should emphasise that - whereas, tests are used, questionnaires are used because it is useful, the expense is not so great. Similarly, no comparisons were made with some other town where war was also being waged, so one was not in a position to differentiate between these two matters. May I now add something that isn't directly related to the question? For example, as I said, if we're investigating one phenomenon and we fail to take into account all the risk factors that lead up to that -- to the appearance of that phenomenon -- for example, if you ask me whether I am a basketball fan, whether I watch basketball matches, and I say sometimes. You might say -- you might come to the conclusion, since it is often said that in my country they are the world champions, you might come to the conclusion that I like to watch basketball. That would be one possible conclusion. But you didn't ask me about other matters, whether there was something that I did earlier on too, and only then would you find out, for example, that since my relative has started practicing training basketball, I start watching basketball more and he always asks me about basketball, so because of my relative I watch a little more basketball than I used to do. So similarly in this investigation we have to take into account all the factors that might be the cause of fear. In my report, I said that it would be most objective if you had a good investigation plan and you had a team of experts who worked on it and who would carry out the necessary research and obtain valid results.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Simply, are you telling us that in Mr. Turner's statement there were no tests conducted in order to measure the intensity of terror, if there was terror, of course? In your practice, in the psychiatric practice, is there a test, is there a procedure allowing to properly quantify in some form - I wouldn't know which one it is - but to quantify somehow what we call terror?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: In psychiatry, there are tests which address fear itself, that is, whether somebody has experienced certain events, the contents of which go beyond everyday human experience, which cause fear and stress. And there we can -- depending on the situation, one can put together a list to have respondents answer whether they were afraid and how much. There are also other questionnaires which tackle the effects of fear. In modern psychiatry there is a lot said about acute stress disorders and post-traumatic stress disorders, and there are some questionnaires too which quantify also the effects of fear once experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, since I'm not an expert, can I then conclude that there are tests which are quantifiable but the question which then follows up is: What is the scale? If you have an experience in that. How can one quantify it? If there is a scale -- for instance, one gives marks from, I don't know, 1 to 10 or something? Is there such a system?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: In medicine in general, in the methodology of medical research, there are things which are measurable, that is, we can measure how much somebody weighs, the number of electrocytes [as interpreted] one has in his blood. That also is measurable. However, when it comes to some other things which, depending on the observer may give rise to a certain subjectivity and depending on the respondents, different scales are developed, and therefore there are terms such as "sometimes," "at times" "frequently", "always", "never." So scales are put together and we have people declaring themselves on individual phenomena, and the same holds true of the sensation of fear and questionnaires that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you could find a suitable moment for a break within two or three minutes. And I would have one small question for clarification of something the witness told us before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question takes two or three minutes, you are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Dr. Kuljic, could you explain to us in not more than two or three minutes what criteria you had in mind when you said that in the report of Dr. Turner the criteria of the Prosecution were introduced. Could you tell us which criteria exactly you meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, concerning the selection of witnesses. Am I making myself clear? I mean, the selection of witnesses. Is that what you are asking me about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that might be. I'm not asking you. You said the criteria of the Prosecution were introduced in the report of Dr. Turner instead of, I would say, objective and general criteria. But if your answer is that Dr. Turner made a selection on the basis of Prosecution witnesses and only studied the statements of them, then that is a clear answer. But I don't know whether you had that in mind. It was just a selection of his sources of what the Prosecution considered to be victims, or was there anything else when you had criteria in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that too, the criteria. Which people will be interviewed, that is, whom will the Prosecution interview and how the Prosecutor will interview them. I apologise. I speak in the first place as a physician, as somebody who is involved in scientific and professional work. And we, therefore, must have an adequate interview or a questionnaire on the basis of which we make our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer until now well when I say it's the selection and the choice of subjects in the interviews or statements used? Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is yet another thing, and that is, for instance, that Dr. Turner also refers to some results which he found in the literature accessible to him. In this accessible literature, and the outstanding point must be that in a large number of cases we do not have representative samples. We have ad hoc samples only. And I also tried to find out as much as possible from medical literature, and I found there findings which do not agree with the findings that Dr. Turner indicates. I can say that that is the product of those random samples which can be different, and the only representative planned sample is something that is, shall we say, nearest the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the third of the criteria is that he used selective material, selective published material to support his opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what he had at his disposal, but I am saying that certain things in his report, there are certain things which speak the opposite. If you wish me, I can give you some examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say he's not completely covering the literature that he could have consulted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, nobody can cover the entire literature. But I'm saying what he quotes in his report, I can also add that there are some other authorities which disagree with what he says there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This clarifies, as far as I'm concerned, your criteria from the Prosecution. If there are any others, please tell us. But perhaps we should first have a break. We'll adjourn until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Dr. Kuljic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, your examination will be continued. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, a while ago, following a question by the President, you said that you were able to find in the literature some other elements which added something to your conclusions. Can you tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Like this: I'd say as I said earlier there are different findings in the available literature. Dr. Turner, in his report, mentions the work of Prato and associates, I think Begovic who says that during the period under consideration in Sarajevo there were 119 killed and wounded. I found that work, and let me add that this was done on the basis of results from the two biggest hospitals. I found another paper which relates to the state hospital on the one hand and a paper which addresses the clinical centre in Sarajevo on the other. And they are, as far as I know, the two biggest hospitals in Sarajevo which was covered by the paper that I have just mentioned, by Prato. However; if one analyses the number of admissions, and they say that a number of these admissions meant wounded, for one of the hospitals I found that if one divides it by the number of days during which they were interviewed, it was 13 per day and in the other hospital, 18 a day, which is a big discrepancy in relation to 119 a day. We have 13 plus 18, is 31. So it's plus/minus one patient, because statistically we cannot divide it into half patients. This is one of the things which, for instance, was significant. I can quote other --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment, Doctor, if you will be so kind. But will you first tell us where did you find these results and how can you be sure that it was done on the basis of original documents, original documents to which your colleague Dr. Turner referred to?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Exactly. I also found one of those papers mentioned by Dr. Turner and those two papers, I found them at the same source, or rather, the same site, which I used -- which I or any of my colleagues used often. So it is a site which in fact is of the United States department for health and human resources - I think that's what it's called - and through that site you can reach the database, that is Pubmed or Medline, that is a database which collects the abstracts of papers from a large number --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have an objection to make in the absence of the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have an objection to make in the absence of the witness. But perhaps before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps before the witness leaves, could it be clarified, because it's relevant to the objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Whether the source was through the Internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you referring to a Internet site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is an Internet site which presumes medical database. I can give you the address. If you like, you can check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We know at least that it's an Internet site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's sufficient for the objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you would like raise the objection in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have to ask you, Dr. Kuljic, to follow the usher for one second and leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we wait until the witness has left the courtroom? Yes. Yes. Usually we'll first listen to the objection and then to the response. But if there is any you consider to be proper to raise before the objection is raised, if it would be something different that would prevail, then please do so. Otherwise, I'd like to hear first the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. What I want to say is that I'm really surprised at the time needed to make this objection. We heard all this answer. Why wasn't it made in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what the objection is about, so I don't know whether it's in the beginning or at the end. Mr. Ierace, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, there was another meeting between the Defence and Prosecution commencing at 12.30 today at which a number of issues were discussed and I invited the Defence to raise any further issue which they wished to. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin said cryptically that Mr. Kuljic had discovered some further material on the Internet and that words to the effect it would be used. I asked him what the material was, and he declined to indicate what it was. Now, I don't know whether this material is the material that Mr. Piletta-Zanin had in mind. We know that this material came to the attention of the witness through the Internet. Mr. President, if the Defence legal counsel is aware of material in the mind of their expert before he enters the witness box, it being material which is not in his report, and they intend to elicit that material and where it is of a technical nature that requires research by the other side, one might think it to be a fundamental principle that that material should be disclosed -- should have been disclosed. In these circumstances, it's my respectful submission that any such material which has already been given by this witness be given no weight and it be made clear to the Defence that they are not to elicit any further material from this witness; in other words, they must rely on what is in his report. In other words, in these circumstances, it was a knowing contravention of a basic principle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Mr. President, I think that it has escaped the attention of the Prosecution that it was following your question that I asked these questions. In effect, that this expert witness was going very far. He told me, and moreover, I've found confirmation, which is very good for the justice, I've found further cooperation for this on the site. And as soon as I could do it loyally, I informed the Prosecution about it. So you see how we are being treated. We are treated like dust to whom anything can be thrown. This is not based on a document but on a consultation. In other words, Mr. President, and I will now -- yes, I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let's leave the strong words out and let's just concentrate on the issue. The issue is that first of all, do you intend to ask further questions about the source the witness just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, on the subject of the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But yes, of course, about the content, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next question would be: If you referred to newly found Internet sources during a meeting with Mr. Ierace, is it true that he asked you what these Internet sources were, as he tells us?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This again is completely false. No, that is completely false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard that you said that his answer -- I do understand that there is a contradictory picture of events, and we heard earlier today that there was another occasion where you and Mr. Ierace contradicted each other in the description of an event. Did you -- if not asked, did you give the source to Mr. Ierace? Did you give the Internet address --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because when, as we were meeting, discussing this morning, I did not necessarily have this information, the information concerned, and that was not the question that was asked by Mr. Ierace. Mr. Ierace asked me - because that is what I remember about it - if this information were the object of regular disclosures under the Rules, to which we're all subject. Mr. Ierace knew that it was not the case and that there was something that the witness intended to indicate to us. But I was not going to say that. And that was the question of Mr. Ierace. It was a matter which had to do with the communication of information, which I did orally as soon as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told Mr. Ierace that new sources were explored by the expert. You were aware that these were Internet sources. Did you know anything about the content of these sources?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask you one question: If you would say I am -- my expert witness has found new sources in a book and if you know, since the expert witness told you what was the content of what we find in that book, would you feel under an obligation to inform the other party of the content of your new knowledge, on the basis of your disclosure obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in principle, yes, insofar as I have time to do it. If I find it out on the very day when something happens, then I simply cannot do everything that is necessary to inform somebody. To say simply this witness has found certain things and we shall see what he says in his testimony, but he is simply verifying finally some scientific articles to which Mr. Turner referred to, and he found it on an Internet site. So he simply is confirming that he has really done his work thoroughly. And for me this is the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two issues, as far as I can see now: First of all, whether there is any additional information on this Internet site, or whether the Internet site should be regarded as a suspicious Internet site because it comes from certain sources, the information comes from certain sources, or the verification of the content of an article mentioned by Dr. Turner. If Dr. Turner mentions a specific article, I think it's irrelevant where you find that article if you want to verify the content of that article and whether Dr. Turner used that correctly or not. And even whether you found it in the book shop, on the Internet or wherever, is hardly of any relevance. You're just verifying the sources used by Dr. Turner. If there's anything else, if there's other information on that Internet site that is relevant, then it might be different. Let me just confer within the Chamber to see what to do with this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be two issues. One is a more or less occasional reference to an Internet site where the source used by Dr. Turner has been found, which this witness verified in order to verify the report of Dr. Turner. There's a -- might be another issue, that is, that on this Internet site additional information has been gathered by this expert witness and that he will testify about that. Until now there was hardly anything more than that reference to an Internet site on which he found an article, although he added something which seems to be the start of a interpretation of the quality of that Internet site. But I'm not -- I mean, whether it's -- where it comes from is not of any importance. If any additional questions will be put which elicit any new information, so going beyond the article being found on that Internet site, but if there's any additional information or whatever on that Internet site, it should have been disclosed and no questions are allowed to that end, at least not at this very moment, since the -- since disclosure obligations are a continuing obligation. This would mean that if there's any relevant material which the Defence would like to deal with during the examination, they should disclose it immediately after this at 7.00 so that we'll see then tomorrow whether any questions will be put to the witness in that respect, and then at least the Prosecution has had some opportunity to prepare, and if the time for preparation has been sufficient, I don't expect any objection -- if there would be any other reasons to object, we'll hear from them by tomorrow. So no specific new information from the Internet site allowed at this very moment. That's how we should deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps I misunderstood you. I would only be half surprised by this. But this witness didn't find an article by Dr. Turner, as I think that you said. It doesn't appear in the transcript. There is a sign which indicates that it wasn't recorded. But I think I heard you say that he had found an article written by Dr. Turner, and this is not the case. This is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that changes your position in any way, although I doubt it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The page 69, line 16, it says, answering your question on the sources, "I also found one of those papers mentioned by Dr. Turner and those two papers. I found them at the same source, or rather, the same site which I use," and then he explains that his colleagues used the same site and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right, Judge Nieto-Navia. But I think that Mr. President spoke about a written article, an article written by Dr. Turner. I think that he spoke about that a minute ago, and that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I did so, that must then have been a mistake. I don't know whether I said it. But I was -- I was referring to an Internet site on which Dr. Kuljic had found an article which appears in the report of Dr. Turner. So questions in respect of that article, being one of the sources, one of the known sources - although now found on the Internet - are permissible. Anything else at this moment is not permissible to ask about. If that is clear to the parties, I'll ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, I don't know if I have understood this correctly, but I'll move on to other subjects and then tomorrow morning we will return to this issue, once we have provided the Prosecution with everything that they have requested. And they will be provided with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be very practical if you would ask the witness - although, we'll not ask at this moment more questions about the Internet site you mentioned - could you please give the address already, the Internet address on which you found one of the articles referred to by Dr. Turner. You said it was something of the US Ministry of health or -- do you have the Internet address of that site or -- yes, could you please give it. Could you tell us what it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that you didn't learn them by heart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'll be glad to explain the technology and tell you how it all functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How what functions? Internet sites or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the -- and all the parties are -- I don't know whether there's any specific technology involved, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it about linking of one site to another site, the technology you are talking about, or what did you specifically have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that it's a database, and there is a way of introducing a key term, a term that you are interested in, and then you obtain a list of all the works, with excerpts where this word appears. If you're interested in the word "heart attack," you put that information in, and then you get all the works, a list of the works relating to this subject. And then you find what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I make a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If the witness has with him the -- a print-off of the relevant document, then perhaps that could be given to Madam Registrar, photocopied overnight, and that might be the most confident way of obtaining the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the paper that you've got in your hand at this very moment is that correct a copy of the material you found or the search results or what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first page -- this is the home page. And here you have the search engine, as you said, and the article itself, well, I have it here. I hope that the fact I have underlined certain parts is not a problem. I can provide you with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might not be a problem for those who read it, but it might be a problem for you, apart from giving the text of a published article also to reveal part of your own thinking, which is -- this is important because most people underline what they deem to be important and other parts not being underlined. But is this other -- are there any other -- is there any other material you've found on that site that you consider to be of relevance for your expertise in this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some other results here. This is not a secret. Anyone who finds this site can have access to this. It's free of charge. Anyone can have a look at this. So my way of thinking was -- my idea was that the entire problem should be addressed in a methodologically correct way, and the literature itself should be able to give opposing results. As I said in the periods that we investigated in those three studies, we find information that does not agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. If you would agree to give a copy of your material to the registry, she'll be able to copy it so that it's available for Prosecution and Defence, so that if there would be any questions about it, that they can be put to you. But therefore, my question was: You said that you had a home page, you had a second page with, I take it, a search engine or something like that on it. And then you had a copy of an article. Do you have more articles printed out from this Internet site that you think to be relevant? Yes. Would you be willing to give them to the registry so that they can be copied, that they can be put at the -- that they can be given to the parties so that whenever there would be a question, it can be put to you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are articles here. There are some articles. I don't know whether they'll be needed at all. I don't know whether the hearing will head in that direction, because there's a large number of articles. This is just a selection. But we can discuss everything. I could bring a computer here and we could carry out searches on the spot. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If you've found certain articles on this Internet site, could you please give them to the registry. They will be copied, the original wills be returned to you. But if the parties think them of relevance, they could put questions to you about them. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, and thank you for your intervention. Can I ask the witness to provide us with all the articles he recently found on this Internet site so that we can copy them and provide the Prosecution with copies, since I think that the witness carried out these searches quite recently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I address you? May I address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are other articles -- as I said, the number of articles is immense. When you type in the word "Sarajevo," you get 577 articles that deal with Sarajevo. That's an enormous number. I have some other articles here. I don't know whether we will deal with them or not, but it's not a problem. I can provide you with these articles, the ones you have asked me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is of any use to provide us with hundreds of articles. Did you discuss the content of some of the articles with Defence counsel? There's nothing against that, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some articles here which are more interesting. And as you said, I worked on this recently. I was looking for certain things which came out this month, last month. Naturally I was getting prepared for my appearance here. We all want to find the truth, determine what the truth is, so I wanted to have as much information as possible. So they are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From a procedural point of view, it's of importance -- no, no, no. Please listen to me for one -- from a procedural point of view, it is of importance that whatever article you discussed with Defence counsel should be known to the other party as well. So you provided us now with the abstracts of three articles. They are not full articles, but they are abstract, as far as I can see. Were there any other abstracts or articles of which -- that you discussed or that you brought to the attention of Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can provide you with the other articles too. It's a summary. They're not excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be at least all the articles you have brought to the attention of Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of the more interesting results that I have here, I can provide them to you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one thing: How many of these articles did you discuss, as far as the content is concerned, with Defence counsel? Were there 10, were there 20, were there 100 or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've printed out about 20 articles, I think. As I said, I don't know. Perhaps I'll later on refer to some article that hasn't even been printed out but I have in my head because I wasn't able to include everything in the written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But of course you can't give any article that you have not yet printed out to the registry at this very moment. But again, how many articles did you discuss from the point of view of the content with Defence counsel? Because this Chamber wants to be sure that whatever you discussed as sources with Defence counsel, that you make it available for the Prosecution as well. That's our major concern at this moment. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a minute just to clarify this matter, because I think I understand what his problem is. It will only take me 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would help. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. I'm sorry for you, Dr. Kuljic, that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understand the reasoning of the witness with regard to this issue, and I have to explain what it is to the Chamber. First of all, the witness and I discussed articles that are well known but haven't been published. I'm thinking about -- I'm referring to the -- to works on Pavlov's dog, things like that, well known to the public. I'm also thinking of the Stockholm syndrome. We discussed these matters. But I think this is a matter of common knowledge. We spoke in a purely abstract manner without referring to any articles. And secondly, we spoke of several issues, Pavlov, et cetera, about behaviourists, about other subjects. We discussed these matters but in a purely abstract and almost intellectual manner. And this had nothing to do with the articles. And secondly, Mr. President, in the excerpts that the doctor is going to speak to us about, he told me what his methodology was and he said, for example, there are 386 articles here but out of these 386 articles, for reasons which he can explain, I made some cross-references and there aren't any that address the issue that is we are interested in, that is to say, Sarajevo and terror. So he spoke about 386 articles, more or less - I don't know the titles of all these articles - but he said if I carry out such a search, I get about 400 answers. He mentioned them, but he wasn't more specific. This is something I can't provide to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of these articles, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the content has not been discussed with you. Just saying that I found 300 sources but they are of no use is not discussing the content. I'm trying to find out what of these documents have been -- well, the content of these documents has been -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's where I'm heading. He said there are 300 articles, but these aren't to be taken into account. But we spoke about, I think, six articles, and the doctor said these articles exist, you should be aware of that. And also, I can tell you when I found out about this - I worked with this doctor no later than this morning - and he spoke to me about it this morning, and it's this morning that I spoke about this to the Prosecution. So I think we're splitting hairs here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, I do understand that there are numerous sources to be consulted, but you discussed some of the articles you found on the Internet site with Defence counsel, the content of these articles. What would be approximately the number of -- or perhaps the precise number of the articles to which you have drawn the attention of the Defence? Would there be two, four, six, eight, ten, twenty, sixty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my discussions with the Defence, I mentioned research. I mentioned the fact that I had worked, and I mentioned 577 articles about Sarajevo, and I went into greater detail about five or six subjects which were of greater importance. And I said that there were articles that confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to have copies of these five or six. If you have them in -- in an abstract form or -- would you have these five or six articles? Could you provide them to the usher so that they can be reproduced and that both parties have similar access to the sources you used in forming your opinion. I've got three here already. I think these are the first three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said five or six subjects and articles that confirmed this, so there will be a greater number of articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But these articles will be stapled together, the ones that are important and that deal with certain subjects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got three here. If you would please collect the others and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seven, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are seven articles that have been joined, seven articles that have to do with certain subjects. For one subject you can always find several articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even lawyers are aware that Internet sources are sometimes very large numbers. If there would be any questions specifically on these subjects you found on the Internet, that will not be today but perhaps tomorrow. We'll see. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Mr. President. I will ask a different question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, within the Yugoslav context, is there a problem that we could call the problem of veterans in relation to Bosnia? For example, one talks about Vietnam veterans. Is there such a problem in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Vietnam syndrome is a syndrome -- is a synonym often used for post-traumatic stress. So according to the diagnostic classifications of the World Health Organization, ICD 10 and DSM 4 of the American Association of psychiatrists, these are classifications, categories that relate to stress, the post-traumatic stress disorder and acute stress disorder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to stop you there. You mentioned ICD 10 and DSM 4. You must understand that we are laymen, and could you explain what ICD 10 and DSM 4 means.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: That means International Classification of Diseases and Diagnostic and Statistic Manual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you have the opportunity of carrying out work with regard to the post-traumatic stress syndrome. I think it's call PTDS in English. Have you had the opportunity to work in this field in the course of your professional experience?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell this Chamber what sort of experience you have in this field of activity.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: As far as my professional experience is concerned, that would include my work with patients. As far as research is concerned, I have participated in research carried out by a team. They were researching risk factors for post-traumatic stress disorder in the case of Bosnian combatants. This was presented at the European congress of psychiatrists in Geneva. I worked on my Ph.D. thesis, and this included acute stress disorder. It included this subject. And we could call this the initial phase of post-traumatic stress disorder. And this was the subject of my thesis. And I also studied the risk factor. So this involves researching the reasons for which certain people develop such post-traumatic stress disorder, whereas other people do not develop such a syndrome, although their experiences were similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, at a certain point in your report you take a fairly well-defined position with regard to the reasons for which certain people do develop such a syndrome whereas others don't. Yet they appear to be in the same situation. For example, in the city of Sarajevo. Could you perhaps summarise your conclusions but at the same time expand on them in order for us to understand them better.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: There are certain risk factors which lead to the appearance of post-traumatic stress and acute stress. These factors are related to the character that people have; for example, whether someone has neurotic personality. And this means that certain people will develop such a syndrome with greater ease than other people. And then there are such characteristics, characteristics such as trait anxiety and this has to do with certain personality types, but this is measured by other tests. So this was proven to be a significant risk factor in my research, a risk factor which would enable us to say that in other populations this could be a risk factor which might lead to such a syndrome. And I said that it's possible to say this because my research was conducted on a sample that I had available to me and it was on this basis that I arrived at certain conclusions. There are also factors such as marital status, educational background, previous mental illness, personality traits such as personality disorders. This also predisposes people to developing post-traumatic stress disorder. So these are characteristics that can influence the development of post-traumatic stress, and naturally the trauma that one experiences is also an important factor, the intensity of the experience, the frequency of the experience, and there are other factors which are also involved. Much research has been carried out to determine biological causes or biological correlations for these disturbances. For example, the hormone status, neurotransmitter status, the activities of the entire neural network.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We might return to the biological aspect, but for the moment I would like you to answer this question: With regard to assessing the terror in Sarajevo, did Dr. Turner's report take into account to a sufficient degree the elements, the factors that you have just mentioned; yes or no? Should he have taken them into account, why? Could you please be a little more specific, please. Please develop this subject. Could you please develop this subject.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC
utterances.text: In Dr. Turner's work, there was no information on these other risk factors for the simple reason that he was provided with what had taken place here in the courtroom, and obviously lawyers are not trained to gather such information, so this wasn't included in his research. There wasn't something that one would usually include in big research projects, for example, certain questions are put, questions that in certain psychiatric tests are called the lying scale, certain questions are put to a patient which represent socially desirable answers, and the purpose of this is to see how honest a person was in answering a question or to find out whether he was answering because he thought it was socially desirable to answer in a certain way. So these are questions put to find out what the credibility of the patients are, the subjects are in a certain research.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I'm looking at the time. I think that we will have to continue with this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, how much time do you think you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can't say because that depends on you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you know how much time has been granted, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But I don't know whether we will be allowed to ask questions with regard to verifying Internet sources or not. So if you say I can do that, it will take a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The parties will be provided with the copies in a couple of minutes. Therefore, the material is available overnight to read. What I've seen, it's not very extensive. It's abstracts. Not calculating the time the witness has spent, unfortunately for him, outside this courtroom, you used 47 minutes until now. 45 minutes were granted. Let's just assume that new issues came up during the information in relation to Internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll be granted tomorrow another 20 minutes, and you can then see whether the Internet issues are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Kuljic, we'll have to stop for today. We'll continue tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. May I instruct you to -- not to speak with anyone, nor parties, nor Judges, nor people in your hotel, about your testimony and the testimony still to be given. I think that if you could wait for three or four minutes, that you'll have your originals back, because they are copied at this very moment. And if the parties would have the same patience, they'll be provided with the copies. We'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Piletta-Zanin please repeat that as the interpreter thought the session -- the hearing had been adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It had been. But if there is something that would immediately ask our attention, then we'll have to reopen the session right away. Otherwise, we'll wait until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it wasn't translated, I'll just do so. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not a problem, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It can wait until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
